..
The Marianas remain pinched between a leading edge of the monsoon 
trough and an embedded col to the north-northeast. Southwesterly 
flow buckling against the col, in addition to upper-level divergence,
is allowing for numerous showers and isolated thunderstorms with 
locally heavy showers this evening. Most of the activity is occurring
over the coastal waters, but a few thunderstorms moving over the 
islands cannot be ruled out. The col will gradually continue moving 
to the northwest, inducing a shift from westerly to northerly winds 
in the coming days, as well as showers tapering down to isolated on 
Labor Day. Later in the week, the easterly trade winds will return, 
possibly remaining light to gentle. Shower coverage for next week may
differ as model guidance hints at a potential circulation developing
to the east of the islands. Due to the high uncertainty regarding 
this pattern, showers top out at 30 percent through the end of next 
week. This will continue to be refined as confidence naturally 
increases with time.

Marine...
Light to gentle westerlies will gradually shift to the north through 
Labor Day, becoming easterly possibly by next weekend. For tonight, 
fresh gusts near heavier showers are possible. Westerly swell 
continues to subside, bringing combined seas of 4 to 6 feet tonight 
down to 3 to 5 feet Monday. There is a moderate risk of rip currents 
along west-facing reefs and a low risk elsewhere.

Tropical Systems...
At 1:00 PM, Tropical Depression 23W was located near 27N136E, about 
285 miles west-northwest of Iwo-To. 23W was moving rapidly north-
northwest at 28 mph. Its maximum sustained winds near its center 
have decreased to 30 mph. 23W is expected to maintain this general
movement with a drastic decrease in forward speed. It is expected to
maintain this intensity through tonight into Sunday, then begin to
weaken, possibly dissipating as a significant tropical cyclone some 
time Sunday as it nears the southern main islands of Japan. 

For more information please refer to bulletins from the Joint
Typhoon Warning Center under WMO header WTPN32 PGTW and from the
National Weather Service under WMO header WTPQ32 PGUM.

Eastern Micronesia...
A drier pattern has now moved into both Kosrae and Pohnpei and
continues at Majuro. As we move through the remainder of the 
weekend, Majuro will remain dry until Monday, when the monsoon 
trough re-invigorates across the Marshalls, increasing POPs
(Probability of Precipitation) to around 30 percent as a weak 
monsoon surge develops. This surge will then spread west, bringing
increased POPs to Kosrae and Pohnpei around Tuesday. POPs then look
to increase around 50 percent for all three locations.

Not much change in the marine conditions. Light to gentle winds will
become occasionally moderate for Majuro and Pohnpei Tuesday, and
occasionally fresh for Kosrae. Combined seas will build slightly,
reaching 3 to 5 feet for Majuro, 4 to 6 feet for Pohnpei, and up to 
7 feet for Kosrae.

Western Micronesia...
A broad area of high pressure is loosely centered over eastern Yap 
State, maintaining fairly dry conditions across Yap and Palau through
early next week. During this period of drier weather, light haze 
sourced from distant wildfires in Indonesia are expected to continue 
across Palau and Yap. Farther east, showers are slow to build across 
Chuuk State as moderate northwesterly convergence alongside the 
monsoon trough remains closer to Pohnpei this afternoon. This band of
convergence gradually shifts westward in the coming days, bringing 
scattered showers and isolated thunderstorms tonight at Chuuk, then 
increases to numerous on Sunday. Shower coverage gradually tapers 
down to isolated to scattered Monday and Tuesday as the feature moves
farther westward, bringing scattered showers to Yap around Wednesday
and Thursday. As the monsoon trough reorients itself next week, 
southwesterly convergence begins to set up across Chuuk around 
Wednesday as well, bringing another increase in scattered showers and
isolated thunderstorms towards the latter half of next week. 

Latest altimetry data shows combined seas have subsided to 2 to 4
feet at Palau and Yap, and 3 to 5 feet at Chuuk. Benign marine
conditions are expected to continue over the next several days, with
seas increasing to 4 to 6 feet around Thursday for Chuuk coastal 
waters due to an increase in southeast swell. Light to gentle winds 
persist over the next several days with an increase in gentle to 
moderate southwesterly winds at Chuuk towards the latter half of this
upcoming week.
